conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___? I'm Dr. ___ from the medical team. I understand you came in with chest pain and shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve had three episodes of chest pressure this week. It radiates to my left arm, and I’ve been getting winded walking just a block.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You have a complex cardiac history—multiple stents, heart failure, diabetes, and you're on warfarin. We’ve reviewed your ER labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had a lot of heart issues over the years. Is this another blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ECG showed some minor changes, but your troponin was normal, which is good—no heart attack right now. However, your INR is 5.7, which is quite high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s not good. I’ve had bleeding issues before. Could that delay anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Because your INR is so high, we can’t do a cardiac catheterization right away. We’ve held your warfarin tonight and will monitor it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what happens now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get a nuclear stress test to see if there’s any new blockage causing your symptoms. In the meantime, you’re on aspirin, Plavix, and Imdur to help with the chest pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my blood sugar? I’m on insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your glucose was 208, which is elevated but manageable. We’ll continue your home insulin regimen—Glargine and Humalog as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want that getting out of control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your stress test came back normal—no signs of ischemia. But given your history and ongoing symptoms, cardiology still suspects a significant blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But the test was normal? I’m confused.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but sometimes symptoms and anatomy don’t fully align. Your echo also looked stable—good heart function. But your INR is coming down, so we may proceed to cath soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So they’ll look inside my arteries?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. If the INR is safe, we’ll do a cardiac catheterization to check for blockages and possibly place a stent if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your INR is now 2.1, which is safe for the procedure. You’re scheduled for cardiac cath tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Will I be awake?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s done under local anesthesia. They’ll go through your wrist or groin and use dye to see the arteries.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if they find a blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll likely open it with a balloon and place a stent. You’ll stay on Plavix and aspirin afterward to prevent clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, just updating you—your cath is confirmed for tomorrow at noon. We’ll start a heparin drip tonight to keep your blood thin, since you have antiphospholipid syndrome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But my INR was high before. Is heparin safe now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because we’re bridging carefully. Warfarin is stopped, heparin starts, and after the procedure, we’ll restart warfarin at a lower dose with Lovenox in between.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, just back from your procedure. You did well. They found an 80% blockage in the mid-LAD—just after a previous stent—and placed a new drug-eluting stent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the other artery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There was a 75% blockage in the OM1 branch. They opened it with balloon angioplasty. No stent was needed there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So both were treated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’re now on dual antiplatelets—Plavix and aspirin—for at least a year to protect the stent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve reported feeling better, and your lungs are clearer. We gave one dose of IV furosemide for mild fluid buildup, but no signs of heart failure worsening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My legs were a bit swollen, but it’s not bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs look stable. Your hemoglobin improved from 11.8 to 12.4—chronic anemia, but not concerning now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my INR?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s 150 now because of the heparin, but that’s expected. We’ve stopped the drip. You’ll go home on Lovenox twice daily and warfarin 5 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Lower than before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, from 2 mg to 5 mg daily. It seems counterintuitive, but your previous dose wasn’t controlling your clotting risk well, especially with antiphospholipid syndrome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ah, okay. I was on 2 mg? That seems low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. So we’re increasing it to 5 mg with close INR follow-up in the anticoagulation clinic next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my heart rate? I’ve been feeling a bit slow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had some bradycardia. Your metoprolol was decreased from 200 mg to 150 mg daily to help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on that for years. Is it safe to lower it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially since you’re on diltiazem too. We want to avoid overly slowing your heart. You’ll follow up with cardiology to reassess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home today. You’ve improved significantly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your medications, especially Plavix, aspirin, atorvastatin, and the new warfarin/Lovenox bridge. Take your nitroglycerin if chest pain returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the oxycodone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re getting a small supply—15 tablets—since you couldn’t refill before admission. Use only as needed for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Cardiology in two weeks, anticoagulation clinic next week for INR. Weigh yourself daily—call if you gain more than 3 pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You did well. Call us if you have chest pain, shortness of breath, or any bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. We’ll see you in follow-up. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your daughter is listed as your healthcare proxy. She has your contact info, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, she’s aware and has everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Discharge papers are ready. You’re free to go when you’re set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it. I’ll get ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy, and we’ll see you soon in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring your prescriptions and discharge instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll wait for her.
